references.text: The psalmist describes idols in a similar way: they have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear, noses but do not smell—the same theme of lifeless gods made by humans.
Nearly identical description of pagan idols as human-made works of silver and gold that cannot see, hear, or breathe.
Isaiah mocks idolatry and describes how people make gods out of wood and metal with their own hands—gods who are powerless.
Jeremiah describes idols as trees cut down in the forest, decorated by craftsmen—they cannot speak, must be carried, and can do neither harm nor good.
Habakkuk condemns those who trust in silent idols made of wood and stone, carved by humans, and asks what use a carved image has.
Revelation mentions that people continued to worship idols made of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood—which cannot see, hear, or walk.
Paul in Athens argues against the idea that the divine resembles gold, silver, or stone shaped by human art and thought.
